title: The 45-minute clock
body:
You get 45 minutes, one sitting, one attempt, and you cannot pause. Assume 4–6 questions on a scenario of roughly 300–500 words plus a data table.

| Minutes | What you are doing | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 0–5 | Read **everything** — scenario, data, and all questions — before writing a word. Underline the numbers. | Question 5 usually reveals what question 1 was really asking. |
| 5–7 | Write a one-line plan per question in your answer boxes. Skeleton only. | If you run out of time, a skeleton still scores. A blank box scores zero. |
| 7–38 | Answer in order, holding a hard per-question budget. With 5 questions that is roughly 6 minutes each. | The single biggest cause of a bad score is question 5 being blank. |
| 38–43 | Sweep back. Add a number where you have none, add a metric where you recommended something, add a risk line. | These three additions are where the marginal marks are. |
| 43–45 | Final read for anything unfinished. Submit with time to spare. | Never trust the last 60 seconds of a browser timer. |

**If you are running out of time**, switch to bullet points immediately. Four sharp bullets score far better than two polished paragraphs and an empty box. Announce it if you like — *"In brief, given time:"* — and then land the points.

**Never** spend 15 minutes on question 1 because you happen to know a lot about it. The marks are distributed across questions, not across your enthusiasm.
checklist: Read all questions before answering any
Write the minute budget down before you start typing
Skeleton every answer box early
Reserve the last 5 minutes for the numbers-and-metrics sweep

title: The answer skeleton — memorise this
body:
The evaluator is reading fast and looking for evidence of structured thinking. Give them a shape they can scan. Use this skeleton for almost any question:

> **1. Verdict.** One sentence that directly answers the question asked.
>
> **2. Diagnosis.** Two or three bullets on *why* it is happening, each anchored to a number from the case.
>
> **3. Recommendation.** Two or three concrete actions, ordered by impact-over-effort, each specific enough that someone could start it on Monday.
>
> **4. Measurement.** The one or two metrics that would tell you within a defined window whether it worked.
>
> **5. Risk.** The main thing that could go wrong, and the trade-off you are knowingly accepting.

### Fill-in template

```text
Verdict: The core problem is [X], driven primarily by [Y].

Why:
- [Metric] fell from [A] to [B], which points to [mechanism].
- [Second evidence], suggesting [inference].
- The thing that is NOT the problem: [rule something out].

What I would do:
1. [Action] - because [reason]. Effort: [low/med/high]. Expected effect: [direction, rough size].
2. [Action] - ...
3. [Action] - ...

How I would know it worked:
- Primary: [metric], measured [how], target [value] within [timeframe].
- Guardrail: [metric that must NOT get worse].

Risk: [main risk]. I am accepting [trade-off] because [reason].
```

Ruling something *out* — "this is not a pricing problem, because X" — is one of the cheapest ways to signal analytical thinking. Most candidates only argue for; arguing against shows you considered alternatives.
checklist: Every answer opens with a direct one-line verdict
Every claim is anchored to a number from the case
Every recommendation has a metric attached
At least one alternative explicitly ruled out

title: Frameworks that earn marks — and how not to look naive
body:
Reciting a framework scores nothing. *Applying* one, and naming it in passing, scores well. Learn these four; use at most one per answer.

### 1. The agentic visibility funnel

The classic marketing funnel does not describe what happens when an AI assistant is the interface. Use this instead:

**Prompt → Retrieval → Citation → Consideration → Action**

- **Prompt** — is your brand even in the space of questions users ask? (Category framing.)
- **Retrieval** — when the assistant searches, does your content come back? (Crawlability, structure, freshness.)
- **Citation** — of what was retrieved, does the assistant actually cite you, and in what position?
- **Consideration** — does the way you are described make a user want you? (Sentiment, accuracy, comparison framing.)
- **Action** — can the user, or their agent, actually transact? (Feeds, APIs, structured availability.)

This is the single most useful diagnostic tool for this theme, because it turns "we are less visible" into "we are failing at stage 3 specifically". *When it makes you look naive:* if you walk all five stages when the case clearly only concerns one.

### 2. Root-cause laddering (five whys, done properly)

Traffic is down → because citations are down → because our pages are not being retrieved → because our content is structured as long unsegmented prose → because we optimised for dwell time in 2019. Each rung must be supported by evidence in the case, or you are just guessing in a formal shape.

### 3. ICE / RICE for prioritising

When asked "what would you do first", score your options rather than listing them: **Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort**. You do not need real numbers — relative high/medium/low with one line of justification is enough and reads as disciplined. *When it makes you look naive:* inventing precise-looking scores like 7.4 with no basis.

### 4. Effort-versus-impact 2×2

Fast to write, easy to scan, and it forces you to commit. Put your recommendations in the quadrants and say which quadrant you are starting in and why. Works especially well when the question asks for a phased plan.

### What to avoid

SWOT, Porter's Five Forces and the 4 Ps will read as padding here. They were not built for this problem and the evaluator will notice you reaching.
checklist: Can you recite the five stages of the agentic visibility funnel from memory?
One framework per answer, maximum
Every framework application cites evidence from the case
No SWOT

title: How to quantify anything in 90 seconds
body:
An answer with numbers beats an answer without, even when the numbers are estimates — **provided you state the assumption**. Evaluators reward visible reasoning, not precision.

### The sentence patterns that earn the mark

> "Assuming X, that implies Y."
> "Taking the midpoint of the range given, roughly Z."
> "Order of magnitude: this is a lakhs problem, not a crores problem."
> "I do not have data on X; if it is roughly Y, the conclusion holds — if it is 10× that, I would reverse this recommendation."

That last one is the strongest sentence in case interviewing. It shows you know which assumption your answer is load-bearing on.

### Funnel maths

If 100,000 people ask a category question monthly, the assistant cites 3 brands per answer, and you appear in 12% of answers, you are visible in 12,000 answer-impressions. If those convert at a third the rate of a direct search click, and your direct-click conversion is 2%, then 12,000 × 0.67% ≈ 80 conversions. Every step there is an assumption, and every assumption is stated. That is a full-marks quantification.

### Converting a share-of-voice delta to money

```text
revenue impact = category prompt volume
               x delta in share of AI answers
               x click-or-action rate from an AI citation
               x conversion rate
               x average order value
```

You will not have all five numbers. Take what the case gives you, assume the rest out loud, and show the multiplication.

### Sanity checks that catch embarrassing errors

- Does the total add to 100% where it should?
- Is the answer within an order of magnitude of the company's stated revenue?
- Would this recommendation cost more than the value it creates?
- Did you compare a monthly number with an annual one?

### Reading the data table

The table is not decoration. It usually contains one deliberate anomaly — a metric moving against the others. Find it, name it, and build your diagnosis around it. Candidates who never reference the table lose marks even when their prose is good.
checklist: At least one quantified estimate per case
Every assumption stated out loud
The data table is explicitly referenced
One sanity check performed before committing to a number

title: Writing for the evaluator
body:
The official criteria are *analytical thinking, strategic approach, and the ability to derive actionable insights*. That is the rubric. Here is what each one actually looks like on the page.

| Criterion | What scores | What does not |
|---|---|---|
| **Analytical thinking** | Reasoning from the data given, ruling alternatives out, spotting the anomaly in the table, stating assumptions | Restating the scenario back; asserting causes with no evidence |
| **Strategic approach** | Prioritised recommendations with a stated reason for the order; acknowledging trade-offs; a phased plan | An undifferentiated list of every idea you had |
| **Actionable insight** | Recommendations specific enough to start on Monday, with an owner, a metric and a timeframe | "Improve content quality", "leverage AI", "increase engagement" |

### Phrases that signal each criterion

- Analytical: *"The anomaly here is…"*, *"This rules out…"*, *"Two readings fit this data; the one I favour is…"*
- Strategic: *"I would sequence this as…"*, *"The trade-off I am accepting is…"*, *"First, because it is reversible and cheap…"*
- Actionable: *"Within two weeks, ship…"*, *"Measured by… against a baseline of…"*, *"Owned by the content team, not engineering."*

### Phrases that lose marks

"Leverage synergies." "Robust omnichannel strategy." "Best-in-class." "AI-powered solution" with no mechanism. "Do a deep dive" with no statement of what you would find. If a sentence would survive find-and-replacing the company name with any other company, delete it.

### Formatting

Short paragraphs. Bold the verdict line. Numbered lists for recommendations, bullets for evidence. White space is not wasted space — it is what makes a skimming evaluator find your structure.
checklist: Verdict line bolded or first
No sentence that would survive a company-name find-and-replace
Recommendations numbered, evidence bulleted
Read once for jargon and delete it

title: Observation versus actionable insight
body:
This is the difference between an average answer and a strong one. An observation describes; an insight tells someone what to do differently and how you would know it worked.

| Weak — observation | Strong — actionable insight |
|---|---|
| "Our organic traffic is declining." | "Organic sessions fell 34% while category demand grew 8%, so this is share loss, not market contraction — the fix belongs to content structure, not to budget." |
| "We should improve our SEO." | "Restructure the top 20 commercial pages into question-and-answer blocks under H2 headings, because retrieval systems chunk on headings; measure by citation rate on our 50 tracked prompts within 30 days." |
| "AI is changing search." | "62% of our category prompts now return an answer with zero clicks, so we should stop optimising for click-through and start optimising for being the cited source inside the answer." |
| "We need better content." | "Our pages answer 'what is X' but users ask 'X vs Y for a 200-person team' — we have no comparison content, which is why competitors get cited on comparison prompts and we do not." |
| "Track brand mentions." | "Sample 100 fixed prompts weekly across three assistants, log which brands are cited and in what position, and alert when our share of voice moves more than 5 points week over week." |
| "Engage with the community." | "Get listed and reviewed on the three sources our competitors are cited from — G2, the two category roundups — because assistants cite aggregators more than vendor sites for comparison prompts." |
| "Use structured data." | "Add Product and FAQPage schema to the 40 SKU pages missing it; this is a two-day engineering task and it is a precondition for shopping agents parsing our catalogue at all." |
| "Monitor sentiment." | "Two of five assistants describe our onboarding as 'slow', traceable to a 2023 review; publish an updated onboarding benchmark page and re-test those prompts in 30 days." |
| "Invest in AI." | "Do not build a model. Build the measurement harness first — you cannot improve visibility you cannot see, and the harness is a two-week build." |
| "Improve the customer journey." | "The journey now starts inside an assistant, so the first controllable touchpoint is our product feed, not our homepage — audit feed completeness before touching the site." |

Read the left column again before your round. Under time pressure, everyone drifts left. The discipline is to write the observation, then ask *"so what would I do about it, and how would I know?"* — and only the answer to that question goes in the box.
checklist: Every observation followed by a 'so what'
Every recommendation has a timeframe
Every recommendation has a named metric
Nothing in the left column of that table appears in your answer

title: Curveball bank
body:
Fifteen questions an evaluator can slip in to see whether you actually understand the problem. Three or four sentences each is the right length.

**1. Is optimising for AI answers just gaming the system?**
There is a real line. Making your content accurate, well-structured and machine-readable helps the user get a correct answer — that is legitimate. Fabricating reviews, spinning doorway pages, or stuffing prompts is manipulation and carries both platform and reputational risk. The test I would apply: would I be comfortable if the user saw exactly what I did to become visible?

**2. What if the assistant describes your product incorrectly?**
First find the source — assistants ground answers in retrievable content, so an error usually traces to a stale page, an old review, or a competitor's comparison article. Fix the source, then re-test the prompt over the following weeks. Most platforms also have a feedback path, but content correction is the durable fix.

**3. Your AI visibility work cannibalises your own SEO traffic. Continue?**
Yes, if the category is moving. Defending a declining channel is more expensive than establishing a position in a growing one. But I would run them in parallel rather than switching, because organic search still carries most of the volume today and the transition timeline is uncertain.

**4. There is no rank tracker for AI answers. How do you measure anything?**
Build a prompt panel: a fixed set of representative prompts, sampled on a schedule across multiple assistants, logging which brands appear and where. It is sampling, not census, so treat it statistically — track the trend and the confidence interval, not a single week's number.

**5. Answers are non-deterministic. Isn't your measurement noise?**
Partly, which is why you sample the same prompt multiple times per period and report a rate rather than a binary. Non-determinism inflates variance; it does not remove signal. Increase sample size until the week-over-week noise is smaller than the effect you care about.

**6. Should we block AI crawlers?**
Only if you are a content business whose product *is* the content and you have a licensing route. For most brands, blocking removes you from the answers your customers are reading — it protects the page view and loses the customer.

**7. Budget is being cut by 40%. What survives?**
Measurement and structured data. Measurement, because everything else is unmanageable without it. Structured data, because it is a one-time engineering cost with a durable effect. Campaign-style content production is the first thing I would cut.

**8. Your competitor is cited more. Is that necessarily bad?**
Not on its own. It depends on *what* they are cited for and whether the citation is favourable. Being cited as the budget option on a premium prompt is worse than not being cited. Segment share of voice by prompt intent before treating it as a scoreboard.

**9. How is this different from SEO?**
SEO optimises for a ranked list a human scans; you win a position. Generative engines synthesise an answer from several retrieved sources; you win a citation and a characterisation. The units change from keywords and rankings to prompts, citations and how you are described.

**10. What would you do in your first 30 days?**
Week 1: build the prompt panel and take a baseline. Week 2: audit structured data and crawler access. Weeks 3–4: fix the top 20 commercial pages for retrievability and ship one comparison page for the highest-volume comparison prompt. Nothing before the baseline, because otherwise nothing is attributable.

**11. Prove the ROI.**
Honestly: attribution here is weak, and I would not pretend otherwise. I would use a holdout — improve one product category and not another — and compare assisted conversions and branded search volume between them. Imperfect, but far better than claiming a causal chain that the data cannot support.

**12. Your recommendation takes six months. The CEO wants results this quarter.**
Split it. Structured data and feed fixes are days, not months, and they move retrievability. Content restructuring is the slow part. I would ship the fast half this quarter with the baseline in place, and be explicit that the compounding effect is next quarter.

**13. What if the platforms change their algorithm next month?**
That is why the durable investments are the ones that are good regardless: accurate, well-structured, freshly-maintained content and clean machine-readable data. I would avoid tactics that depend on a specific retrieval quirk, because those are the ones that get patched.

**14. Where does this sit organisationally?**
It cannot sit only in SEO, because half the fixes are engineering (feeds, schema, crawler policy) and half are content. I would put the measurement harness with a data owner and give a single accountable person the share-of-voice number, with a working group across content, engineering and PR.

**15. If you could only track one metric, which?**
Share of citations on a fixed panel of high-intent category prompts, weighted by citation position. It is the closest single number to "when a buyer asks an assistant about this category, do we show up first" — and it moves before revenue does.
checklist: Can you answer curveballs 1, 4, 9 and 11 from memory?
Practise saying 'I don't have that data, here is what I'd assume'
Have a 30-day plan ready to deploy on any case

title: Score your own practice answer
body:
Grade yourself honestly out of 20 after each practice case. Under 12 means rewrite it rather than moving on.

| # | Criterion | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Answers the question actually asked | Drifted onto another topic | Partially | Directly, in the first line |
| 2 | Uses the data given | Never referenced it | Quoted a number | Interpreted the anomaly |
| 3 | Quantification | None | One vague number | Estimate with stated assumptions |
| 4 | Causal reasoning | Asserted | One 'because' | Chain of reasoning, alternative ruled out |
| 5 | Prioritisation | Flat list | Ordered | Ordered *with the reason for the order* |
| 6 | Specificity | Generic advice | Somewhat specific | Startable Monday, with an owner |
| 7 | Measurement | Absent | Named a metric | Metric, baseline, target, timeframe |
| 8 | Risk / trade-off | Absent | Mentioned | Named and consciously accepted |
| 9 | Domain credibility | Generic marketing | Some correct terms | Mechanism-level understanding |
| 10 | Structure and scannability | Wall of text | Some structure | Verdict, bullets, clean skeleton |

**16–20** — shortlist-grade. **12–15** — solid, usually losing marks on quantification and measurement. **Below 12** — the content is probably fine and the structure is failing you; rewrite using the skeleton before writing anything new.
checklist: Score every practice answer before reading the model answer
Score it again after, and note which two criteria you lost most on
Those two criteria are your prep focus
